lesson.title: One Thread, Many Sockets: select() and poll()
lesson.summary: select() and poll() are the classic POSIX system calls that let a single thread ask the kernel which of many sockets are actually ready to read or write, but both carry real scalability costs as connection counts grow.
lesson.body:
Non-blocking sockets solve the problem of a single slow connection stalling a thread, but they leave open a practical question. With dozens or hundreds of sockets open, how does a program know which ones are actually worth checking right now, without wastefully calling recv() on every single one over and over? select() and poll() are the two classic POSIX answers. Both let a thread hand the kernel a list of file descriptors it cares about and ask, in one call, which of them are currently readable, writable, or have an error pending. The thread then only touches the sockets the kernel reports as ready, and if nothing is ready yet, the call itself blocks, with an optional timeout, so the thread sleeps efficiently instead of spinning.

select() is the older of the two. It takes its set of file descriptors as fixed-size bitmasks, called fd_set, one bit per descriptor, and on many systems this is capped by a constant called FD_SETSIZE, historically 1024, meaning a process cannot ask select() to watch more file descriptors than that limit, no matter how many it actually has open. poll() was introduced to remove that hard cap. Instead of bitmasks, it takes an array of pollfd structures, one per socket the caller wants to watch, with no fixed ceiling on how many can be included.

Both calls share the same underlying scalability limitation, though. Every time either is called, the caller has to pass its entire list of watched file descriptors, and the kernel has to walk that entire list to check the status of each one, even if only one or two sockets out of a thousand actually have anything new to report. That is an O(n) scan on every single call, where n is the total number of watched sockets, not the number that are actually active. As the number of connections a server holds open grows into the thousands, this scanning cost, together with the cost of copying that whole list between user space and kernel space on every call, starts to dominate, since most of the work is spent re-examining sockets that have not changed since the last check. This is part of what became known as the C10K problem, the difficulty of a single server efficiently handling ten thousand concurrent connections using tools designed for far smaller numbers.

For moderate numbers of connections, a few hundred at most, select() and poll() work fine, and they have the advantage of being available essentially everywhere sockets are. But once a server needs to hold open many thousands of mostly idle connections, a common shape for things like chat systems or long-lived API connections, the repeated O(n) scanning becomes the actual bottleneck, not the network itself. That gap is what epoll and kqueue were built to close.
